name: Iris Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee carpenter for Meadowgate Homes on a new estate on the edge of town, three hundred houses, all about six designs. I go round with a fixer called Tony hanging doors, fitting staircases that come pre-made from the factory, and doing skirting and boxing-in for pipes. I'm the slowest on the team, but Tony says I'm the tidiest. I like that the houses are for families like mine, first-time buyers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home and how you came to this.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I left school before my exams to help in my dad's corner shop when he was ill. At twenty-three I wanted my own trade, and my uncle knew a site manager, so I got on a carpentry programme. I live with my parents and my grandmother, which is how I've saved about five months of money. I use AI sometimes, mostly because my younger brother showed me how to ask it about fixing details, but I'd rather ask Tony.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, hard work still counts for something. I wouldn't post anything, I'd just mention it at home. Dad would say he's been saying that for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep learning and keep my head down. Meadowgate always needs carpenters on these estates. I'm not worried about AI in that world, more about doing my job well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going with Tony and finish my apprenticeship assessments by next autumn. Keep saving for a flat of my own. Help Dad in the shop on Sundays like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you about Meadowgate, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that they keep using more factory-made bits. Staircases used to be built on site, and now they arrive in one piece. The housebuilder I work for, Meadowgate, already buys staircases ready-made, so I'm learning a trade that shrinks a little every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your family? Your dad's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's shop is quiet since the supermarket put in self-checkouts nearby. He's sixty and talks about selling. But he says the family will manage, and I believe him.

say: I'd say **hard work** still counts for something in this world.
I'd mention it **at home** over dinner rather than posting anything.
think: Meadowgate **always needs carpenters** on these big estates.
My focus is on **doing my job well** and learning from Tony.
do: Keep saving for **a flat** of her own.
Keep helping in **Dad's shop** on Sundays.
S0.quote: The housebuilder I work for, Meadowgate, already buys staircases ready-made, so I'm learning a trade that shrinks a little every year.
fieldNote: Living with family gives her a **five-month** cushion.
She notices **factory-made parts** quietly shrinking site carpentry.
Her dad's shop faces **self-checkout** pressure, a family worry.

steps.text: Finish her carpentry apprenticeship assessments by next autumn
Keep saving monthly for a flat of her own

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should learn a trade and stay useful. Changes come, and the ones who work hard adapt. I'd say it to my cousins who are always on their phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it makes me a bit nervous. The site office will plan everything on computers and order straight from the factory. I'd guess Meadowgate pushes even more of the house into the factory, which means less on site for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my assessments, but I'd ask Tony to teach me the jobs factories can't do, like fitting stairs into odd spaces or fixing mistakes. I'd try the AI app for checking measurements, once Tony's comfortable with it. I'd keep saving the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I feel the ground move a bit, but I'm still standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Tony say about this kind of change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My trainer Tony says builders have always been told a machine is coming, and Tony has hung doors for thirty years. He's not wrong, but he's also near retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever look at a different kind of building work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe repairs and maintenance for housing associations. Old houses, broken doors, leaky windows. Those don't come out of a factory.

say: I'd say people should **learn a trade** and stay useful.
I'd tell my cousins that **hard workers adapt**.
think: Meadowgate will push **more into the factory**, leaving less on site.
The **site office** will plan and order everything by computer.
do: Ask Tony to teach **awkward-space fitting** and fixing mistakes.
Try the **AI measuring app** once Tony's comfortable.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, the ground moving a little.
S1.quote: My trainer Tony says builders have always been told a machine is coming, and Tony has hung doors for thirty years.
fieldNote: She sees the **factory**, not AI itself, as her main threat.
She looks toward **repairs and maintenance**, where every job differs.
She takes up new tools **after her mentor** does.

steps.text: Ask Tony (her fixer) to teach awkward stairs and repairs
Try the AI measuring app once Tony uses it
Keep saving monthly for a flat at the same rate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can't wait for the government to fix this. Families and communities have to help each other. I'd say it at the temple and at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm one of the first to go. By 2028 the planning and ordering is all done by computer. By 2031 the robots arrive, and a big estate builder like Meadowgate would buy them first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the assessments as fast as I could, then move into repair work for a housing association. I'd save almost everything and stop buying clothes and meals out. I'd talk to Dad about whether the shop could become something different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like being told the bus I'm on won't stop at my stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the estate has six designs. Why does that matter here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three hundred houses in six designs is the easiest job in the world for a robot to learn. Every door is the same height, every staircase the same shape. That's why I think Meadowgate goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would say we'll manage as a family. Mum would worry. My grandmother would pray. I'd tell them I've got savings and a plan, even if I'm scared.

say: I'd say **families and communities** must help each other.
I'd say it **at the temple** and at home.
think: Volume builders like Meadowgate would **buy robots first** by 2031.
I'm one of the **first to go**, as a junior on standard houses.
do: Rush the **assessments**, then move into housing association repairs.
Save almost everything and stop **clothes and meals out**.
Talk to Dad about **changing the shop**.
feel: She feels **alarmed**, like the bus won't stop at her stop.
S2.quote: Three hundred houses in six designs is the easiest job in the world for a robot to learn.
fieldNote: She spots that **standard house designs** are easy for robots.
She expects to **lose her job** at Meadowgate by 2031.
Her family is the safety net, with **prayer and pooling** money.

steps.text: Rush her assessments and apply for housing association repair work
Stop buying clothes and meals out to protect her savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so let's plan. I'd tell the younger ones to get a trade that needs judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to qualify and get a few years as a carpenter. By 2034 I'd want to be in repairs, where every job is different. But Meadowgate's estates will still go to robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship on time and move to a housing association repairs team within two years. I'd keep saving for my flat. I'd probably try the AI tools more, since they'd help with repair quotes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see the path. It's less like a bus and more like a train with a timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the five years that you couldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Choose where I go instead of being pushed. Five years lets me walk out of Meadowgate (the housebuilder she works for) on my own terms instead of being shown the gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want your own flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but maybe later. I'd rather have a steady job first, even if it means staying at home till thirty.

say: I'd say there's **time to plan**, so let's plan.
I'd tell younger people to get a **trade that needs judgement**.
think: Five years gets me **qualified** and experienced before robots in 2034.
Meadowgate's big **estates** will still go to robots in the end.
do: Finish the apprenticeship and join a **repairs team** within two years.
Use **AI tools** more for repair quotes.
feel: She feels **anxious** but can see the path.
S3.quote: Five years lets me walk out of Meadowgate (the housebuilder she works for) on my own terms instead of being shown the gate.
fieldNote: Extra time means she can **choose** when to leave Meadowgate.
She'd delay **moving out** until work is steady.
She'd use AI more once it **proves useful** for repairs.

steps.text: Join a housing association repairs team within two years
Delay moving out until work is steady
Use AI tools to write repair quotes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning. Work hard, learn properly and you'll be all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty for me to become a good carpenter. I'd move to repair work, maybe even run a small team. I'm not too worried with that much time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now for a year: assessments, saving, Sundays in the shop. Then, around year three, move to a repair team. I'd keep up with AI tools slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you like to be in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I want to be leading a repairs team, with a flat that's mine and my parents proud. That's the dream, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year picture that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's shop, honestly. Whatever happens with AI, the shop is fading now. I'd want to help him close it without losing too much.

I'd say **work hard** and learn properly, and you'll be all right.
think: Ten years is plenty to become a **good carpenter**.
I could even **run a small team** in repairs.
do: Keep doing her assessments and **Sundays in the shop** this year.
Move to a housing association **repair team** around year three.
feel: She feels **mostly fine**, with a little unease.
S4.quote: By 2036 I want to be leading a repairs team, with a flat that's mine and my parents proud.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets her plan a **repairs career**.
Her lasting worry is **Dad's shop** fading, not AI.
Faith and family remain her **anchors** across all scenarios.

steps.text: Keep helping in Dad's shop on Sundays

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I'd be the first to go at Meadowgate. Robots love straight walls and the same door six hundred times, and that describes every estate I've ever worked on. What would help is apprenticeships in repair work and help for families like mine to change together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about older parents. People like my dad, sixty, with a shop that's already dying. Nobody's going to retrain him, and he's too proud to ask.

headlineQuote: Robots love straight walls and the same door six hundred times, and that describes every estate I've ever worked on.
portrait: Iris is a 27-year-old **trainee carpenter** on a large volume housing estate.
She lives with her **parents and grandmother**, saving about five months of money.
She's **traditional**, valuing family, faith and hard work over government help.
She sees **factory-made parts** and standard designs as making her job easy to automate.
She plans a move into **repair work**, which feels safer with more time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as volume builders adopt robots first and juniors go.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships in repair work** and help for families to change together.
